The major 19th-century territorial acquisitions: Louisiana Purchase (1803, referenced), annexation of Texas (1845), Oregon settlement (1846), and the Mexican Cession via the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848)

claims.claim: 'Manifest Destiny' was an ideology/belief, not a fact or an actual destiny: the phrase was coined by journalist John L. O'Sullivan in 1845 editorials and expressed the claimed God-given right and duty of White Americans to seize and settle the West, spreading Protestant, democratic values.
The United States purchased the Louisiana Territory from France in 1803 for $15 million.

The United States annexed the former Republic of Texas by joint resolution (passed March 1, 1845) and admitted it on December 29, 1845; Texas had won independence from Mexico in 1836. The Oregon boundary with Britain was settled at the 49th parallel by the Oregon Treaty of 1846.

The Mexican-American War (1846-1848) ended with the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, signed in February 1848, under which Mexico ceded a vast territory (the Mexican Cession: California, Nevada, Utah, and most of Arizona and New Mexico, plus parts of Colorado and Wyoming) - roughly half of Mexico's national territory; the U.S. paid Mexico $15 million and assumed $3.35 million in claims.

Gold was discovered at Sutter's Mill in Coloma, California on January 24, 1848; the mass migration of 'forty-niners' followed in 1849, bringing more than 100,000 migrants to California within about a year of the discovery.
Congress passed the Indian Removal Act in 1830, mandating removal of American Indian nations east of the Mississippi to lands in the West (Indian Territory, present-day Oklahoma).
In Worcester v. Georgia (1832) Cherokee leaders won a favorable Supreme Court ruling, but President Jackson's administration refused to enforce it and removal proceeded.

The Treaty of New Echota (signed 1835, ratified by the U.S. Senate in May 1836) was signed by about twenty Cherokee men, none of them elected tribal officials; it purported to cede all Cherokee land east of the Mississippi for $5 million and new lands in Indian Territory.

In 1838-1839 the U.S. government forcibly removed more than 16,000 Cherokee from their homelands in Tennessee, Alabama, North Carolina, and Georgia to Indian Territory; the last detachments arrived on March 24, 1839. This forced removal is known as the Trail of Tears; roughly a fifth of the Cherokee people (commonly estimated around 4,000) died from exposure, disease, and the hardships of relocation.

The Cherokee were not the only nation removed: the Indian Removal Act drove the forced removal of southeastern nations including the Choctaw, Muscogee (Creek), Chickasaw, and Seminole, part of a systematic pattern of broken treaties and displacement across the era of westward settlement.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The exact number of Cherokee deaths on the Trail of Tears
positions: NPS teaching materials estimate that nearly one-fifth of the Cherokee population died
A widely cited figure is approximately 4,000 deaths
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as an estimate ('thousands', 'roughly a fifth', 'commonly estimated around 4,000') rather than a single exact number, matching the range in the sources.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft was placeholder boilerplate ('Expansion is a foundational concept in History...') with no substantive historical content; nothing in it was usable as evidence.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire boilerplate draft with a researched, date-verified lesson.
Reframed Manifest Destiny explicitly as an ideology used to justify expansion, not as fact or inevitability, and named its racial/nationalist assumptions.
Centered the Native American experience (Indian Removal Act, Trail of Tears, broken treaties, Worcester v. Georgia) rather than telling a settler-only story.

Facts synthesized; prose original.

sourceRecords.title: The Trail of Tears and the Forced Relocation of the Cherokee Nation (Teaching with Historic Places)
sourceRecords.notes: Verified: Treaty of New Echota (ratified May 17, 1836; signed by ~20 men, none elected officials) ceded Cherokee eastern land for $5 million and Indian Territory; Cherokee won in the Supreme Court but Jackson refused to enforce; forced removal primarily 1838-1839, last detachments arrived March 24, 1839; nearly one-fifth of the Cherokee population died.

sourceRecords.title: Trail of Tears National Historic Trail
sourceRecords.notes: Verified (NPS trail pages, read via search excerpts of nps.gov): Indian Removal Act of 1830 mandated removal of tribes east of the Mississippi; in 1838 the government forcibly removed more than 16,000 Cherokee from Tennessee, Alabama, North Carolina, and Georgia to Indian Territory (present-day Oklahoma); the trail spans about 2,200 miles across nine states. Supports the Indian Removal Act date and the broader removal of southeastern nations.

sourceRecords.title: The Discovery of Gold (Early California History: An Overview)
sourceRecords.notes: Verified (via LoC/allied sources): gold discovered at Sutter's Mill, Coloma, January 24, 1848; President Polk's December 1848 announcement triggered mass migration; the 'forty-niners' arrived in 1849. Read via search excerpt of the LoC essay.

sourceRecords.title: The California Gold Rush (California National Historic Trail)
sourceRecords.notes: Verified: gold discovered January 24, 1848 kicked off one of the largest mass migrations in history, with more than 100,000 people arriving in California within the first year, from Europe, Asia, the Americas, Australia, and New Zealand. Read via search excerpt of nps.gov.
